touches.text: Tool: a complete primitive. Has users, not an owner. Calls no other Cairn component (stdlib and base only) and owns no state of its own. Lives in cairn/tools/ (17). Its data for a holder lives under that holder: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/.
PURPOSE: Python sieves run over a build; reds a component that fails one (no charter, no proofs, a silent device, ...). "We find a new thing, we add a new sieve."

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception. Akien 2026-11-13, on Q#88: "over the bus. that's what it's for?"

The inspectors are not assumed correct; they are examined when they refuse. After a gate refuses, an LLM sets the refusing sieve's intention and why beside the ticket's intention and why and asks: is this sieve the best we can do right now? If yes, the ticket changes. If no, the sieve is fixed through its own ticket and proof. Either way the system improves. WHY: a disagreement becomes an update to an intention or its implementation, never a conversation about procedure. The sieves stay deterministic and never weigh a why; the LLM check comes only after a failure, and it is never a lock pick because it has no third outcome. Nothing passes a ticket over a red.

Every sieve carries its own why, and the why names where it came from. Akien designed the inspector tools; CC built each specific sieve from what it read him to mean. So the adjudication in 17.11.6 is against the sieve's own why, done by CC, and never a question to him. Akien 2026-11-13: "I designed the tools, but not the specific sieves. you built those to handle what you thought i meant for each inspector. ... i don't know why each sieve is there. we are supposed to add a why to each sieve so we can help adjudicate it. and this is also why the sieves are not perfect. Nothing in this system ever will be perfect. the whole thing will constantly be under improvement." Measured that day: build_inspector registers 43 sieves, and the 36 sieves/*.json records carry name, band and dials but no why. The whys live only in docstrings.

The same boundary runs wherever Akien designed a tool or machine and CC filled in its specific contents: the nest and its questions, the inspectors and their sieves, the gates and their checks, the corrosion set, the skill doors and their field lists. Each such component's charter carries a design_boundary naming what Akien designed, what CC designed, and how a red over CC's part is settled. CC's part is CC's to adjudicate against its own why. Akien may be asked whether a part could be better, with the whys laid out, and whatever CC can't sort goes to him. A new component that has this boundary declares it in its charter when it is born. Akien 2026-11-13: "i think we make a note in the nest and/or sieve tools/machines that the specific contents are at your design. and anywhere else we wind up with an akien/claude boundary. because i'm aware I hadn't thought about that boundary until today."
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

The RULE 1 check is a path check: code inside device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo (anything not under cairn.devices.bar), except a tool foo publishes (cairn.devices.foo.tools.<x>, its charter saying published_by_device). Inside one device there is one owner, so nothing is checked there. A charter's public_interface describes what the component offers (modules, functions, bus verbs, commands); the check does not read it. Akien 2026-11-09 (Q#77): "wouldn't it be easier (for the python code anyway) to see if the imports do not include other device paths?"
